title: Reverse Linked List
description: Brute force to optimized: extracting values and rebuilding versus in-place pointer flipping with a running prev/curr pair.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list, and return the new head.

blocks.caption: Flip each node's next pointer backward, one node at a time

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","The head of a singly linked list"],["Output","The head of the same list, with every node's next pointer reversed"],["Goal","Reverse the list in a single pass, in place, without creating new nodes"],["Constraints","The number of nodes is in the range [0, 5000]; -5000 <= Node.val <= 5000"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Every node's \"next\" pointer needs to point BACKWARD instead of forward","A running \"prev\" pointer, tracking the already-reversed portion built so far"],["Overwriting a node's next pointer would lose the rest of the original list","Save the \"next\" node in a temporary variable BEFORE overwriting the current node's pointer"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the direction of every node's next pointer, so the list reads in the opposite order, and return the new head (the original list's last node).

blocks.title: Analogy: Flipping a Line of Dominoes to Point the Other Way
blocks.text: Like walking down a line of dominoes, each currently pointing to the one after it, and flipping each domino to point to the one BEFORE it instead, one at a time. Before flipping any domino, its original "points to" direction must be remembered first, since flipping it destroys that information immediately.

blocks.caption: prev tracks the reversed portion; curr.next is flipped to point at prev, then both advance

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: head = [1,2,3,4,5]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Flipping every node's next pointer to point backward: 1<-2<-3<-4<-5","Reversed order: 5,4,3,2,1","The last node (5) becomes the new head, and every arrow now points the opposite way"],["Answer","[5,4,3,2,1]","The fully reversed list"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: head is empty or has only 1 node
An empty list reverses to itself (still empty), and a single-node list reverses to itself as well, since there's nothing to flip relative to.
5. How Should We Think?

Before extracting every value and rebuilding the list in reverse order, notice that each node's next pointer can simply be flipped in place, one at a time, as long as the rest of the list isn't lost in the process.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Reversing the list really just means: for every node, its next pointer should point to whatever was BEFORE it, instead of what comes after it.

Observation 2: Walking through the list while maintaining a "prev" pointer (the already-reversed portion built so far, starting as null/None) lets each node's next pointer be flipped to point at prev directly.

Observation 3: The moment curr.next is overwritten to point at prev, the ORIGINAL next node would be lost forever unless it was saved first, in a temporary variable, before the overwrite happens.

Observation 4: After flipping curr's pointer, prev advances to curr (since curr is now the head of the reversed-so-far portion), and curr advances to the saved next node, continuing the process until curr becomes null.

Recognizing that flipping a next pointer requires SAVING the original next node first (before it's overwritten) is the one crucial ordering detail that makes this simple, single-pass in-place reversal work correctly.
This is the classic iterative in-place linked list reversal technique: maintain a running "prev" pointer, and flip each node's next pointer to point at it, always saving the true next node first.
6. Brute Force Solution
Extract every value into a plain array, reverse the array, then build an entirely new linked list from the reversed values.
Step by step algorithm

items: Walk through the original list, collecting every node's value into an array.
Reverse the array, then build a brand new linked list from the reversed values.

codes.python:
def reverse_list(head):
    values = []
    node = head
    while node:
        values.append(node.val)                                            # collect every value into a plain array
        node = node.next
    values.reverse()                                                       # reverse the array itself
    dummy = ListNode(0)
    cur = dummy
    for v in values:
        cur.next = ListNode(v)                                             # rebuild a brand new linked list from the reversed values
        cur = cur.next
    return dummy.next


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(3, ListNode(4, ListNode(5)))))
    result = reverse_list(head)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Values are collected first, since reversing requires knowing the full sequence before flipping its order.
A brand new linked list is built from the reversed values, since this brute force does not reuse any of the original nodes.
The dummy head simplifies building the new list, avoiding special-case logic for the first node.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every value is collected and correctly reversed, so the resulting list is always accurate.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), one pass to collect values plus one pass to rebuild.
Space: O(n), for the intermediate array and the entirely new set of nodes created.

Limitation: extracting values and creating brand new nodes ignores that the EXISTING nodes' next pointers can simply be flipped in place, achieving the same result with no extra node creation and O(1) extra space.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force creates entirely new nodes. Instead, walk through the original list once, maintaining a "prev" pointer (starting at null) representing the reversed portion built so far. At each node, save its true next node in a temporary variable, flip the current node's next pointer to point at prev, then advance both prev and curr forward by one position each.

Initialize prev to null and curr to head. While curr is not null: save next = curr.next, set curr.next = prev, then set prev = curr and curr = next. Once curr becomes null, prev holds the new head of the reversed list.
9. Optimized Solution
Flip each node's next pointer to point at the running "prev" pointer, always saving the true next node first.
Dry run for head = [1,2,3,4,5]

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: curr becomes null, ending the loop; prev is now 5, the new head, with the chain 5->4->3->2->1->null, matching the expected reversed list.

codes.python:
def reverse_list(head):
    prev = None                                                             # the already-reversed portion built so far (starts empty)
    curr = head
    while curr:
        next_node = curr.next                                              # save the rest of the original list before overwriting curr.next
        curr.next = prev                                                   # flip this node's pointer to point backward
        prev = curr                                                        # curr becomes the new head of the reversed portion
        curr = next_node                                                   # advance to the next unprocessed node
    return prev


if __name__ == "__main__":
    head = ListNode(1, ListNode(2, ListNode(3, ListNode(4, ListNode(5)))))
    result = reverse_list(head)
    values = []
    while result:
        values.append(result.val)
        result = result.next
    print(values)

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass through the list.
Space: O(1) extra, reusing the existing nodes and only 2-3 pointer variables.
Why This Works

prev always represents the head of the correctly-reversed portion of the list built so far. Saving curr.next into a temporary variable before overwriting curr.next = prev preserves access to the rest of the original (not-yet-reversed) list, which would otherwise be permanently lost the instant the pointer is flipped. Repeating this flip-and-advance step for every node, in order, correctly reverses the entire list by the time curr reaches null.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["curr is not null","Save its true next node, flip curr.next to point at prev, then advance both prev and curr"],["curr becomes null","The loop ends; prev now holds the head of the fully reversed list"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: next is saved as a local variable at the very start of each loop iteration, BEFORE curr.next is ever modified.
prev starts at null, correctly giving the ORIGINAL head's new next pointer (null, since it becomes the new tail) once it's processed.
The function returns prev (not curr), since by the time the loop ends, curr is null and prev holds the actual new head.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (extract values, rebuild)","O(n)","O(n)","Creates an entirely new set of nodes from the reversed values"],["Optimized (in-place pointer flipping)","O(n)","O(1) extra","Reuses the existing nodes, flipping their next pointers directly"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

In-place linked list reversal is a fundamental building block: maintaining a running "prev" pointer and flipping each node's next pointer, always saving the true next node first, achieves O(1) extra space reversal, reusable as a subroutine in many harder linked list problems.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting to save curr.next BEFORE overwriting curr.next = prev, which permanently loses access to the rest of the original list.
Returning curr instead of prev at the end, which is always null once the loop terminates.
Confusing which pointer represents "already reversed" (prev) versus "not yet processed" (curr), leading to incorrect pointer assignments.

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["head is null (empty list)","The loop never executes; prev stays null, correctly returning an empty list"],["head has only 1 node","That single node's next becomes null (unchanged, since it has no next originally either), and it is correctly returned as the head"],["All nodes have the same value","The reversal still works correctly, since it operates on pointers, not values"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly state why saving curr.next first is essential before flipping the pointer, since this exact ordering detail is the most common subtle bug interviewers watch for in this classic problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Reverse a linked list, ideally in place" points toward the iterative prev/curr/next pointer-flipping technique, achieving O(1) extra space.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you reverse it recursively instead? Recursively reverse the rest of the list first, then fix up the current node's pointers (set head.next.next = head, then head.next = null), returning the new head found by the deepest recursive call.

How would you reverse only a SUBSECTION of the list (between two given positions)? This becomes Reverse Linked List II, requiring careful handling of the boundaries just before and after the subsection being reversed.
How would you reverse the list in groups of k nodes at a time? This becomes Reverse Nodes in k-Group, applying this same reversal technique repeatedly to each group of k nodes.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: The foundational iterative pointer-reversal technique, directly reused (with added boundary-handling complexity) in Reverse Linked List II and Reverse Nodes in k-Group elsewhere in this category.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n) time, O(n) space.
Optimized (in-place pointer flipping): O(n) time, O(1) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Iterative in-place reversal using a running prev/curr pointer pair
Core Idea: Flip each node's next pointer to point at the already-reversed portion (prev), always saving the true next node first before overwriting
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: The original next node must be saved in a temporary variable before its pointer is overwritten, or the rest of the list is lost forever
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: next=curr.next; curr.next=prev; prev=curr; curr=next
